newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu camp looks for Zaire election deal.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu camp looks for Zaire election deal.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko's entourage, its future in Zaire threatened by a relentless rebel offensive, is looking for an election deal from Saturday's talks at sea between Mobutu and civil war rival Laurent Kabila.

With Kabila insisting that the veteran strongman must go, Mobutu's son and spokesman Nzanga side-stepped questions on his father standing down and said he expected the meeting on a South African ship would lead to further negotiations.
Both Nzanga and Honore Ngbanda, Mobutu's security advisor and hitherto chief negotiator, envisage elections for all.
But Kabila, whose forces control over half the sprawling Central African nation and are marching on the capital Kinshasa, remains adamant -- the veteran strongman must go.

"The agenda will be discussed and I think following that meeting there will be other negotiations that will bring I hope a peaceful transition that will lead to elections," Nzanga Mobutu told British Broadcasting Corporation's African service.
Critics accuse the president and his entourage of milking what is potentially Africa's richest nation and amassing fortunes while Zaire's people remained mired in poverty.
The talks were scheduled for Friday but were put off until Saturday because the harbour in Libreville, Gabon, cannot accommodate the ship they plan to meet on, Nzanga told Reuters.
The meeting will take place on the South African navy ship in international waters in the Atlantic off the coast of Central Africa.
Nzanga said Mobutu and his team would travel to neighbouring Congo on Friday and the meeting would be launched from the Congolese port of Pointe Noire.

Mobutu, who is debilitated by cancer, agreed on Wednesday to meet Kabila face-to-face on the South African naval vessel in international waters, after lengthy meetings with U.S. troubleshooter Bill Richardson.
His clan, its hold on the sprawling nation broken by rebel advances, is anxious to retain a stake in the future of the mineral-rich nation.
But Kabila said on Wednesday that the talks, chaired by South African President Nelson Mandela, would only discuss the departure from power of Mobutu, Zaire's ruler for 32 years.
"The talks will just be about Mobutu and what we do with him. Our uncompromising demand is that he leaves power and we shall look after him," Kabila told Reuters.
Kabila's forces, who took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, control over half of Zaire and are marching on Kinshasa.
Nzanga Mobutu said the president's entourage expected the talks to lay the groundwork for negotiations on a transitional arrangement leading to elections.
"No matter what he (Kabila) says, there must be elections. Elections are not only about President Mobutu, elections are about the Zairean people," he said.

"The future of Zaire goes beyond the very person of President Mobutu. Whatever decision he makes will talk about the future of Zaire and I hope Mr Kabila has something to give the Zairean people," he added.

Ngbanda told Radio France International that he expected the talks to build on earlier contacts. He said these covered "a ceasefire, the desire of the two sides to organise a peaceful transition leading to transparent and democratic elections that exclude no-one."
Both Nzanga and Ngbanda brushed aside suggestions that Mobutu was ready to quit or that the talks were about providing him with a face-saving way out.
"What do you mean by quitting?" Nzanga asked.
